extracted.intended_audience: literary critics, poets, and students of poetry
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating and producing poetic diction, style, and the critic's method — emphasizing naturalness, imagination, grammatical/psychological grounding, and fair critical practice. Applies to assessing individual poems and a poet's characteristic voice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction of rhyme and metre versus poetic diction
rubrics_metrics.description: “The distinction of rhyme and metre is regular and uniform, and not, like that produced by (what is usually called) poetic diction, arbitrary, and subject to infinite caprices...” (discussion of how metre can often be rendered as prose, while rhyme affects final words).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Meter can often be transcribed into prose with little alteration; rhyme may demand substituting final words of similar meaning, dignity, and euphony. But beware: bad taste or madness can equally spoil rhyme and metre; neither form alone guarantees good poetry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Style governed by principles (grammar, logic, psychology) — Taste
rubrics_metrics.description: “By the principles of grammar, logic, psychology. In one word by such a knowledge of the facts, material and spiritual, that most appertain to his art...and acquires the name of Taste.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A poet's language should be controlled by sound knowledge of grammar, logic, and the human psyche; ignorance or neglect of these principles indicates someone unfit to be called a poet. Taste is the internalized application of those principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language of feeling determined by imagination/meditation, not mere copying
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet should distinguish appropriate language for suppressed versus indulged anger, or between rage and jealousy, 'not by wandering about in search of...people in uncultivated society,' but 'by the power of imagination proceeding upon the all in each of human nature. By meditation, rather than by observation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poetic diction should arise from imaginative insight into universal human nature and meditative synthesis, not from literal transcription of overheard colloquial speech or provincialism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of affected rhetorical caprices (pseudopoesy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Exclude 'the madness prepense of pseudopoesy, or the startling hysteric of weakness over-exerting itself' — forced apostrophes to abstract terms and contrived juxtapositions (e.g., Odes to jealousy, Hope, Oblivion) are to be rejected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrived surprise produced by arbitrary juxtaposition of incompatible images is a species of wit or willful artifice, not genuine imagination. Such devices imply leisure and self-possession incompatible with the fervour of true poetic genius.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imagination's rules cannot be imposed externally
rubrics_metrics.description: “Could a rule be given from without, poetry would cease to be poetry, and sink into a mechanical art. It would be morphosis, not poiaesis. The rules of the Imagination are themselves the very powers of growth and production.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not attempt to substitute external, formulaic rules for the internal generative principles of imagination; prescriptive formulas risk turning poetry into mechanical production.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of the 'neutral' or conversational poetic style (natural dignity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Garve/Gellert praised verses 'in which everything was expressed just as one would wish to talk, and yet all dignified, attractive, and interesting; and all at the same time perfectly correct as to the measure of the syllables and the rhyme.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A style that reads like natural conversation yet attains dignity and metrical correctness is a high excellence; it makes a greater impression than ornate or affected diction. Examples cited include Spenser (in parts), Chaucer, and George Herbert.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical/pronunciation authenticity for naturalness
rubrics_metrics.description: To judge naturalness in older poetry one must 'adopt the pronunciation of the poet and of the court, at which he lived...with respect to the final e and to the accentuation of the last syllable.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apparent oddities in diction or rhyme may be resolved by adopting contemporaneous pronunciation/usage; critics should consider historical linguistic practice when assessing naturalness and euphony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognizability and individuality of an author's diction
rubrics_metrics.description: A person familiar with an author's works will often recognise short quotations as belonging to that author ('a similar peculiarity...attends Mr. Wordsworth’s style...'); distinctive voice and recurring phrasing are merits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characteristic, individual diction which makes a poet's lines identifiable is praiseworthy; overly rigid adherence to a prescribed neutral style could erase such individuality and many of the poet's marked beauties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate elevated vocabulary where necessary for precision
rubrics_metrics.description: In works like THE EXCURSION 'the number of polysyllabic (or what the common people call, dictionary) words is more than usually great,' which is needed 'in proportion to the number and variety of an author’s conceptions, and his solicitude to express them with precision.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use polysyllabic or learned words when they serve precision and complexity of thought; their presence is justified by conceptual need, not by mere ornament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legitimacy of poetic syntactic devices (asymartaeton, apposition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Frequent poetic constructions include the asymartaeton (omission of the connective before the last item) and appositional constructions ('to him, a youth').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such syntactic peculiarities are valid stylistic tools; excising them would eliminate many of the marked beauties of certain poets. Critics should judge these devices by their effects, not by a priori prose norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment by independent striking passages (quotability)
rubrics_metrics.description: Many of Wordsworth’s lines can be quoted without reference to their poems 'for their own independent weight or beauty' and these striking passages form a large proportion of his poems' value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One metric of poetic merit is the frequency and heft of passages that stand alone as memorable; critics may note how often such passages recur and their contribution to a poet's overall worth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fair and philosophical method of criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: A fair criticism 'announces and endeavours to establish the principles, which he holds for the foundation of poetry in general, with the specification of these in their application to the different classes of poetry...particularize the most striking passages...notice the frequent or infrequent recurrence of similar merits or defects...distinguishing what is characteristic from what is accidental.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics should state their canons, apply them class-by-class, cite exemplary passages, report recurrence of merits/defects, and separate characteristic traits from accidents; this makes judgments transparent, testable, and useful to readers and authors alike.
